guidance: Use it when ss, netstat or lsof are missing - a scratch container, a chroot, a busybox or distroless image - and the kernel's own socket table is all you have. Paste the rows as /proc prints them, header and all. The inode in the last column is what ties a row to a process: it appears as socket:[N] among that process's open files, and the page shows the one-liner that finds it. In a UDP table the state reads 07 while the socket is unconnected and 01 once connect() fixed its peer.
method: The /proc row has no labels, so the page locates the first token shaped like an address:port pair and then requires every column after it to match its own shape, which is what keeps a pasted header or a shifted row from being read as data. The kernel prints the address as one 32-bit word for tcp and udp, or four 32-bit words for tcp6 and udp6, with %08X straight from the socket's stored __be32 field rather than in network order, and the port as %04X; on a little-endian host the four octets of each word therefore read backwards, so 0100007F is 127.0.0.1, 3500007F is 127.0.0.53 and 00000000000000000000000001000000 is ::1. The decoder reverses the octets of each word and then formats IPv6 in RFC 5952 canonical form - lowercase, no leading zeros, the longest run of two or more zero groups collapsed, the first run winning a tie - and prints an IPv4-mapped address in mixed notation as ::ffff:a.b.c.d, which is why an IPv6 endpoint comes back bracketed with the port after the bracket. Column 4 is the low byte of the kernel's sk_state enum: the page carries the thirteen values from include/net/tcp_states.h, and because a UDP socket keeps the same enum it reads 07 (CLOSE) while unconnected and 01 (ESTABLISHED) once connect() fixed its peer, so udp mode relabels those two and flags every other code as unexpected. tx_queue:rx_queue is converted from hex to bytes, tr:tm->when to the timer state plus jiffies, retrnsmt to a count, and uid, the probes-out column and the inode are read as decimal. The page accepts the full eleven-column row, the short local/remote/state form and a lone endpoint, skips a header line and counts it, and refuses a row whose fields do not line up with the column name and the value that failed instead of shifting the rest by one. The seven debug fields after the inode - reference count, a zero pointer, retransmission timeout, delayed-ACK control word, congestion window and slow-start threshold - are counted but not interpreted. Everything is computed locally with integer arithmetic: no network access, uploads or storage.

sources.title: Linux kernel documentation, The /proc/net/tcp and /proc/net/tcp6 variables: the annotated row layout used by the column reference, including the transmit and receive queues, the timer and jiffies fields, the uid, the probe counter, the inode and the debug tail.

proc_pid_net(5) from the Linux man-pages: /proc/net/tcp and /proc/net/udp hold the kernel hash slot, the local and remote address and port, the socket status, the queue sizes, the timer fields and the effective UID of the creator.
Linux kernel include/net/tcp_states.h: the sk_state enum read by the page, TCP_ESTABLISHED = 1 through TCP_BOUND_INACTIVE = 13, with TCP_CLOSE = 7 and TCP_LISTEN = 10.

Linux kernel net/ipv4/tcp_ipv4.c, tcp4_seq_show: the seq_printf that writes each row as %4d: %08X:%04X %08X:%04X %02X %08X:%08X %02X:%08lX %08X %5u %8d %llu, which fixes the column order and shows the address printed from the stored field rather than in network order.

RFC 9293, Transmission Control Protocol: the state names and transitions behind the st column and the state table, and the reason a listener, a TIME_WAIT socket and a half-open connection are distinguished.
